analysis.one_liner: Extends federal deposit insurance to cover up to $10 million in business checking accounts at banks and credit unions.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill in February 2026, but the full Senate has not voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Today the FDIC insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor. This bill would add a separate guarantee of up to $10 million for noninterest-bearing transaction accounts — the checking-style accounts businesses use for payroll, rent, and operations — at banks and credit unions. Big Wall Street banks and foreign bank branches are excluded from offering it, and smaller banks and credit unions would not have to pay any special assessment to cover the new insurance during a ten-year phase-in period.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses, nonprofits, municipalities, and other organizations that keep large no-interest checking accounts gain the most: today they can lose everything above $250,000 if their bank fails, and this would insure up to $10 million of those balances. Community banks and credit unions also gain a tool to attract and keep large depositors, and they would be temporarily spared any new assessments to fund the coverage. Ordinary households gain little directly, since their deposits are already insured up to $250,000 — though the bill aims to prevent the kind of contagion where a mid-sized bank failure wipes out local employers' payroll accounts.

how_it_helps.text: It would guarantee up to $10 million per depositor in noninterest-bearing transaction accounts at banks and credit unions, so a payroll or operating account would be fully covered even if the institution failed.
It phases the new coverage in over ten years under an FDIC-written plan, giving the insurance funds time to absorb the added exposure.

It bars regulators from letting banks or third parties structure accounts to evade the limits, and excludes the largest systemically important banks and foreign bank branches from offering the extra coverage.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of the expanded insurance would eventually fall on the FDIC and credit union insurance funds, which are funded by bank assessments — and ultimately backstopped by taxpayers. During the transition, small banks and credit unions would be exempt from paying assessments tied to the new coverage, pushing more of the cost toward larger banks and the funds themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bank insurance funds and, ultimately, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Extending insurance to accounts of up to $10 million shifts the risk of large-account failures onto the FDIC's insurance funds, which are funded by banks and, in a crisis, ultimately backstopped by the government — a cost that could fall on taxpayers or be passed to bank customers.

The additional coverage applies only to accounts that pay no interest, so ordinary households gain little: the standard $250,000 per-depositor limit already covers nearly all personal deposits, and banks have an incentive to keep the expanded coverage tier low- or no-interest.

Community banks and credit unions are temporarily shielded from any increase in assessments to cover the new insurance during the transition, meaning the largest depositors get protection while the smaller institutions' share of the cost is deferred for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for ordinary households is small because their deposits are already insured up to $250,000; the real beneficiaries are businesses, nonprofits, and governments with large checking balances, plus community banks that get the added coverage without paying special assessments during the transition. The cost — added risk borne by the FDIC's insurance funds, which are ultimately backstopped by the banking system and taxpayers — is real but was moderated here by capping coverage at $10 million, phasing it in over ten years, and excluding the largest Wall Street banks. It is a reasonably targeted design, though its main work is protecting business operating accounts rather than people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a hearing on it in February 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Hagerty introduced the Main Street Depositor Protection Act on October 9, 2025, with Sen. Alsobrooks as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
On February 5, 2026, the Banking Committee held hearings on the bill; it has not been reported out of committee or voted on by the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has won or lost; the bill sits in committee. If it never advances, large banks and existing deposit arrangements keep the status quo, while businesses with big checking balances go without the extra protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored by a Republican senator with a Democratic original cosponsor; no opposing votes or statements appear in the record.

industries.note: They get a new tool to attract large business deposits and are explicitly shielded from any special assessments to pay for the expanded coverage during the transition period.

industries.industry: Globally systemically important banks and foreign bank branches
industries.note: The bill bars these large institutions and foreign bank branches from offering the new $10 million coverage, directing the benefit toward smaller lenders.
The funds take on additional insurance exposure for large accounts, but the $10 million cap, aggregation rules, and ten-year phase-in limit that exposure.

industries.industry: Large business depositors (payroll, operating, and government accounts)
industries.note: Businesses, municipalities, and nonprofits holding large no-interest checking balances gain certainty that their funds are fully covered in a bank failure.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one hearing and a single cosponsor; most Senate banking bills at this stage never reach the floor unless the committee chairman advances them or they attach to a larger package. Its odds this Congress are low, though a bank-failure scare or community bank lobby support could revive it.
